AccessRecordRequest.description:
Who read what, for which purpose — the ledgered access event.

Two ways to name the reader, one preferred (D-AG7):

* ``actor_did`` — the structured identity of the component that performed the
  read (a holder's or app's service DID today; an agent's DID once agent
  identities exist). Preferred, because a DID can be authenticated and
  aggregated: "what did this actor do this week" is answerable from it.
* ``accessor`` — the legacy free-text label (``"node0:agent:weekly-synthesis"``).
  Still accepted and still recorded, so existing callers keep working; free text
  can be neither verified nor grouped, which is why it is the one being replaced.

At least one must be present. During the transition both are recorded when both
are sent.

``consent_id`` names the grant the read was made under, when the reader knows
it: a data source has it from introspection (``consent_id`` on an active
access token). Optional, so every existing caller keeps working; when it is
present the ledger entry carries it, so an access can be read back to the
grant that allowed it (sandbox partner finding, 2026-10-04). It is checked for
shape only, against the form this service mints; whether such a grant exists
is not checked, because the ledger records what the caller asserted.

consent_id.description: The grant the read was made under (`urn:lifecare:consent:<32 hex>`), when the reader knows it.
consent_id.title: Consent Id

AgentManifest.description:
**Defined, not yet registrable.** What an AI client declares about itself
(healthspannode `docs/personal-agent-and-multiparty-ledger-design.md` §5.1
D-AG6a; `docs/provider-ehr-context-and-portability-design.md` §6.2, D-PE5).

A manifest is a *declaration*, not a measurement: nothing here is attested by
the network, which is exactly why `trust` and the grant sit above it. The
ladder is the ceiling (D-AG6b: T0 resolvable → T1 vouched → T2 attested,
carried as `trust`, the same three values
:class:`DelegatedTokenIntrospection` already publishes, so there is one
spelling of an agent's tier in the contract and not two), the person's grant
is the floor, and a client can never receive more than the smaller of them.

The two fields the provider-EHR design adds are `hosting` and `egress_class`,
and the rule binding them (§13a, the tightening of D-PE5) is the hard
constraint written as a validator: **outside the box the node sends
categorical envelopes only, and no grant lifts that.** Values leave in one
way: through the write fence into the EHR, where a clinician relied on them.
From the chart they travel under the provider's own legal basis, with the
network not in that path.

There is no registration route. This is published so a holder, a practice
node and a client vendor agree on the shape and the refusals before the first
manifest exists, exactly as the delegated token shape was published ahead of
its issuance.

post.description:
Create a grant on the server-to-server channel.

Two gates, each with its own flag and each fail-open only in its default
position (F1/F2):

* **who is calling, and for whom**: a holder signature, confidential-
  client credentials or the member's own session, verified whenever
  presented, required when ``require_caller_auth`` is on; with it on, the
  caller must be the member or a first-party client;
* **who approved it**: the subject's device proof over the canonical
  grant digest, verified whenever presented, required when
  ``require_grant_proof`` is on, except for the narrowed first-party
  exemption (``caller_auth.may_grant_without_proof``).

And one rule with no flag of its own: a grant naming a grantee in
``member_only_grantees`` is accepted from the member alone
(``caller_auth.require_member_for_grantee``), checked first.

post.description:
Grant a partner access to scopes for a purpose, as the session user.

**Named exemption (F1), narrowed 2026-09-28 (W0-5).** When
``require_grant_proof`` is on, a grant with **no device proof** is accepted
here only when its grantee is first party: an id in
``Settings.first_party_grantees`` or the member's own DID. The session
behind it was minted by a passkey ceremony, so the person is present, and
the panel client has no proof plumbing yet. A grant to anyone else needs
the device proof, because a session is not held by the member alone: every
relying party that signs the member in receives one (security review
P2-2), and before the narrowing any of them could grant any party through
this route. A proof the panel *does* send is verified exactly as anywhere
else, and the remaining gap is written down in ``docs/security-audit.md``.

post.description:
A holder registers / versions / tiers / moves / shreds a resource.

Who may write (security audit F11, operator ruling of 2026-10-04):

* **the member's own node**, a client in
  ``LIFECAREID_FIRST_PARTY_CLIENTS`` presenting its client credential
  (HTTP Basic): its own entries (``holder.id`` is its client id) in any
  ``holder.role`` but ``user_device``, and source entries
  (``holder.role: source``, a provider id as ``holder.id``), for any
  member;
* **a signed holder** (``X-LifeCare-Signature``): only entries whose
  ``holder.id`` is the DID that signed, in any ``holder.role`` but
  ``home_node`` and ``user_device``, and only for a member who has an
  active grant naming that DID as grantee;
* **the member's own device** (their session, ``Bearer lcs_...``, or a
  signature by their own DID): only their own ``user_device`` entries,
  ``holder.id`` their DID;
* **anyone else** writes nothing: no credential is ``401``, any other
  caller ``403``, both before the subject DID is looked up and before
  anything is written or ledgered.

So ``home_node`` ("Your home node" in the member's ledger) is written
only by the member's own node, and ``user_device`` ("Your device") only
by the member's own device.

This holds in every deployment: it does not depend on
``LIFECAREID_REQUIRE_HOLDER_SIGNATURE`` or
``LIFECAREID_REQUIRE_CALLER_AUTH``. A credential that is presented is
verified (a bad signature or client secret is ``401``). An admitted
write for a subject lifecare.id does not know is ``404``.

401.description: No credential was presented, or a presented one failed (a bad signature, a wrong client secret). Checked before the subject DID is looked up.

403.description: The caller may not write this entry: a client that is not first party, a first-party client writing an entry that names neither itself nor a provider source, or a user_device entry; a holder writing an entry that names another holder, a home_node or user_device entry, or for a member with no active grant naming it; or a session writing for another member or anything but its own user_device entries. Checked before the subject DID is looked up.

404.description: An admitted caller wrote for a subject DID lifecare.id does not know.

get.description:
The chained resource history for a DID, newest first, keyset-paginated
on ``entry_hash``.

Who reads what (security audit F11, operator ruling of 2026-10-04):

* **the member**, with their own session (``Bearer lcs_...``) or a
  signature by their own DID: every entry (``read_as: "subject"``);
* **a signed holder** (``X-LifeCare-Signature``): only the entries whose
  ``holder_id`` is the DID that signed (``read_as: "holder"``). A holder
  with no entries for this DID gets an empty page, whether or not the DID
  is registered. ``before`` must be one of the holder's own entries.
  ``chain_valid`` checks each entry shown against its real predecessor in
  the member's chain, so it means the same as in the member's view;
* **anyone else** reads nothing: no credential is ``401``, any other
  caller (a client, another member's session) is ``403``, both before the
  DID is looked up.

This holds in every deployment: it does not depend on
``LIFECAREID_REQUIRE_HOLDER_SIGNATURE`` or
``LIFECAREID_REQUIRE_CALLER_AUTH``. A credential that is presented is
verified (a bad signature or client secret is ``401``).

oneOf.description:
**Defined, not yet issued.** An actor exercising a subset of a subject's
authority (D-AG4b; RFC 8693 actor-claim semantics).

Semantics a resource server must implement before the first one is ever
minted:

* The actor acts **for** the subject, never **as** the subject. A delegated
  token can no more satisfy a "the caller is the user" check than an access
  token can; `subject_did` here names on whose behalf the actor acts, not who
  the caller is.
* Scope, purpose and expiry are bounded by `parent_grant` and can never
  exceed it. No token of any type can create, widen or extend a grant; only
  the person can, through the passkey ceremony.
* Revoking the delegation kills the token and leaves the parent grant intact.

No issuance path exists, so introspection cannot return this shape today. It
is published so resource servers branch on `token_type` now.

scope.description: a single scope, as an access token carries
scope.title: Scope

subject_did.description: on whose behalf the actor acts
subject_did.title: Subject Did

schema.title: Response Introspect V1 Token Introspect Post

200.description: Token status. `token_type` distinguishes the shapes: `user` (the caller is this user), `access` (an app may read this scope), and `delegated` (an actor acting for a subject inside a grant — defined here, never issued today). A resource server must fail closed on any `token_type` it does not implement.

401.description: No client credential was presented, or a presented one failed (a wrong or unknown client secret, a malformed Basic value, a bad holder signature). Answered before the token is looked up, so the answer is the same for every token.

403.description: The caller authenticated, but not as a client: a member's session or a holder signature. Answered before the token is looked up.

429.description: Too many requests for this route from this client (or, on the routes that send mail, for this mailbox) inside the window. Sent only while the deployment's rate limits are on (`LIFECAREID_RATE_LIMITS=enforce`); carries `Retry-After` in seconds. See docs/developers/security-and-compliance.md, Rate limits.
